FLASHCARD SET · AGES 2–6 YEARS

Classroom flashcards.

Thirty cards that name the room school happens in. Eighteen of them are the things your child sees every morning — the backpack, the desk, the whiteboard, the little clock on the wall — and twelve are the good habits every classroom runs on: listening, raising a hand, sharing, saying please and thank you, walking feet inside. Point at the card, then find the real thing; say the habit, then try it today.

Every card in the set.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Name it, then find it

    Pick an object card, say its name, then hunt for the real thing — the clock on the wall, the backpack by the door. Real-object matching is how the words stick, and the hunt is the whole game.

  2. 02

    One habit a week

    Spread the good-habit cards face up and let your child choose the week’s habit. Act it out once, then catch them doing it for real and name the card out loud — "that was SHARING!"

  3. 03

    Pack the backpack

    Use the backpack, notebook, pencil and crayons cards as a packing list for the real bag. Each card checked off is one thing packed by your child, not for them.

  4. 04

    Set up a mini classroom

    Line up a chair and a desk, stand a book beside them, and let stuffed animals be the class. Your child plays teacher with the cards — explaining a rule is the fastest way to learn it.

      Backpack Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The bag that goes to school and comes home — the backpack holds everything a school day needs, and packing it is a child’s very first job.

      Say it together

      “Backpack! This is your backpack. Where does it go? On your back! What goes inside? Snack — in! Bottle — in! A picture you made — in! Zip, zip. Off we go!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pack the real bag together tonight: one thing to eat, one thing to drink, one thing to show. Each item goes in with its name — "snack… in!" — and the zip click ends the ritual. Same time every evening, and packing becomes your child’s job, not yours.

      Quick parent note

      Packing a bag is sequencing: a plan, in order, finished. Children who pack their own bag walk into school a little taller, because the day starts with something they did all by themselves.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Notebook Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The navy notebook with the spiral edge — the notebook is where every mark, squiggle and first letter lands, one page after another.

      Say it together

      “Notebook! Open the notebook. A page for you, a page for me. Draw a line… draw a circle… look what the pencil did! Turn the page — more paper waits!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Start a two-minute notebook habit: one page a day, anything your child likes — scribbles, circles, a letter they are working on. Date the corner for them. In a month, flip back to page one together and count how the marks changed.

      Quick parent note

      A notebook shows progress better than any poster: yesterday’s page sits right beside today’s. Keep the first one safe — the earliest pages become family treasures faster than anyone expects.

      Pencil Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The yellow pencil with the pink top — the pencil is the tool writing starts with, and holding it is a skill the hand learns one grip at a time.

      Say it together

      “Pencil! The yellow pencil. Pinch it near the point — thumb, finger, finger. Make a dot… a line… a wiggle! The pencil talks when your hand moves.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Try "pencil races": you draw a slow line, your child draws a fast one; you draw a circle, they try one. Big paper, fat grip, no corrections — the goal is a hand that wants to come back tomorrow, not a perfect letter today.

      Quick parent note

      Grip grows in stages — fist, then fingers, then the grown-up tripod grip. A shorter pencil actually encourages finger use, so a half-used pencil is a fine first writer for small hands.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Crayons Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The box of rainbow sticks — crayons are color a child can hold, and the box is usually the first color words a child ever uses out loud.

      Say it together

      “Crayons! Open the box. Red… blue… green… yellow! Which one today? Push the paper — look, COLOR! The crayon paints with your hand.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pick three crayons and play color match: one scribble on paper, then hunt for one real thing in the room that color. Red scribble — find red! Three rounds is a full game, and it clears the table of every crayon but three.

      Quick parent note

      Naming colors comes after sorting them, so let matching lead and words follow. Broken crayons are fine — in fact small pieces push little hands toward the finger grip the pencil will need later.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Eraser Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The navy and white eraser — the eraser teaches the quiet lesson every learner needs: marks can change, and trying again is part of the work.

      Say it together

      “Eraser! The rub-a-dub block. Oops went wrong? No tears — rub, rub, rub… and the paper is blank again! Try again. That is what the eraser is for.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Draw a wobbly line on purpose, hand over the eraser and let your child rub it out — the rubbing itself is excellent hand work. Then say the magic sentence together: "wrong lines are how right lines start."

      Quick parent note

      An eraser is resilience you can hold. Children who are allowed to erase are more willing to start — which matters far more than the line they first drew.

      Ruler Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The yellow ruler with its row of numbers — the ruler draws the straight lines and quietly shows that things have length you can count.

      Say it together

      “Ruler! The straight-edge stick. Hold it flat… line it up… draw along the edge — a STRAIGHT line! Wiggle the ruler, draw again — a new straight line!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Go on a straight-line hunt: find three straight things in the room (the table edge, a book, the floor tiles), lay the ruler along each, then draw one straight line of your own. Curvy things are allowed too — the ruler just says no to them politely.

      Quick parent note

      A ruler is early measuring: numbers live on it in order, and every straight line it draws is a tiny lesson in careful hands. Drawing along an edge is real pencil control practice in disguise.

      Scissors Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Classroom object

      The blue scissors with open blades — scissors are the big-kid tool of the craft table, and learning to use them safely is a skill worth practising slowly.

      Say it together

      “Scissors! Thumb on top, two fingers below — open… close… open… close! The scissors only cut paper. Sit down to cut. Slow snips make the line.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sit side by side and cut a strip of paper into scraps — the snipping matters more than the shape. Say the rules out loud each time: paper only, sitting down, walking never. Grown-up eyes stay close by the whole time, and the scissors live up high afterwards.

      Quick parent note

      Child-safe scissors, paper only, seated, with a grown-up nearby — that is the whole rule set, and it deserves saying out loud every single time. Cutting builds more hand strength than almost any other craft tool.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Glue Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Classroom object

      The glue stick with the navy cap — glue is how separate pieces become one picture, and twisting the cap is half the fun.

      Say it together

      “Glue! Twist the cap… round and round. Dot, dot, dot on the back — press it down… push… pat! Stuck! The glue holds your art together.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Tear an old magazine page into pieces and glue the pieces into a new picture — tearing and pressing are both good hand work. One dot per piece keeps the sticky mess friendly; a "dot, dot, not a lot" chant keeps it that way.

      Quick parent note

      Glue teaches "just enough" — too little and nothing holds, too much and everything slides. That judgement call, made on paper at three, is the same one made at the craft table for years.

      Desk Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The little desk with the yellow top — the desk is where work lives, and having a work spot of your own makes starting ten times easier.

      Say it together

      “Desk! This is the work desk. Sit down, feet flat, paper ready. At the desk we draw, we build, we write. All done? Push in the chair — the desk says thank you!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name one spot at home "the desk" — the kitchen table corner counts perfectly. Work happens there, one activity at a time, and the crayons live in a cup on it. Same spot every day turns "time to work" into an easy sentence.

      Quick parent note

      A named work spot does the reminding for you: the place itself says "we work here." Children settle faster when the spot, the light and the materials are always the same.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Chair Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The child’s chair with the yellow seat — the chair is where a body learns to sit for stories, snacks and work, feet steady and back tall.

      Say it together

      “Chair! Sit on the chair. Bottom on the seat, feet on the floor, back tall like a tree. Look — sitting like a big kid! The chair holds you while you work.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play "show me sitting": chair, floor, cushion — which one is the sitting spot? Then sit for one short story and stand up when it ends. Sitting well is a skill with a finish line, not a rule for the whole day.

      Quick parent note

      Expecting a three-year-old to sit still forever is a losing game — short, honest sittings work. Feet that reach the floor (or a box) make sitting comfortable enough to last.

      Teacher’s Desk Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Classroom object

      The big desk at the front of the room — the teacher’s desk is where the grown-up keeps the day’s plans, the stickers and the pens that are not for borrowing.

      Say it together

      “Teacher’s desk! The big desk. Whose desk is it? The teacher’s! Papers live here, stickers live here, the plan for the day lives here. It is polite to knock and ask.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Pretend play is the game: your child sits at a table being the teacher, you raise your hand and ask a question. Swapping roles lets a child see the room from the other side — and teachers-in-training suddenly love rules.

      Quick parent note

      Knowing whose things are whose is real classroom skill: the teacher’s desk is where children learn to ask before taking, one polite request at a time.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Whiteboard Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Classroom object

      The big whiteboard on its stand — the whiteboard is where the whole room can see the idea at once, and every mark wipes clean for the next one.

      Say it together

      “Whiteboard! The big board. A marker for the grown-up… what shall we draw? A sun! A two! Your name! Rub, rub — all gone! The whiteboard waits for the next idea.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Big paper works as a home whiteboard. Draw giant letters together — arm movements first, then marker strokes — and let your child wipe it "clean" with a cloth. Wiping is the reward, and it is also serious hand work.

      Quick parent note

      Whiteboard work is big-movement writing: whole arm, wide strokes, no pressure on the letter shape yet. Giant and messy first, small and neat much later — that is the order writing grows in.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Bookshelf Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The shelf of standing books — the bookshelf is the quiet corner of every classroom, where books wait spines-out for the next little reader.

      Say it together

      “Bookshelf! The book house. Books stand up here like friends on a shelf. Pick one… sit down… open it slowly. Finished? The book goes back in its spot, ready for tomorrow.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Turn one shelf at home into the bookshelf: books standing, spines out, at your child’s own height. The game is the return trip — story finished, book back in its slot. A shelf a child can reach is a shelf a child will use.

      Quick parent note

      Front-facing or spine-out, a reachable shelf gets books chosen far more often than a high one. Tidying a shelf back to rights is also a matching game the child can actually win.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Globe Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Classroom object

      The little world on its stand — the globe is the Earth itself, small enough to spin, and it answers the biggest early question: where are we?

      Say it together

      “Globe! The whole world, tiny! Here is the water — so blue. Here is the land — so green. Spin it slowly… round and round, just like the Earth does. Where are we? Right here!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Spin the globe (or the map on a screen), stop it with a finger, and name whatever is under it — ocean, land, ice. Then find your own home and put a sticker on it. One sticker, one place, one very proud child.

      Quick parent note

      A globe makes "the world" a real thing a child can turn — big ideas need small models. Spinning it also quietly teaches that the world turns, which is exactly the kind of fact four-year-olds love to repeat.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Map Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Classroom object

      The map with green continents hanging on the wall — a map is the world drawn flat, and reading one starts with simply pointing.

      Say it together

      “Map! The world on paper. The blue is water. The green is land. Point to the water… point to the land… point to where we live! A map knows where everything is.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hang any map at child height and play "point and name": one finger, one place, one word each. Draw a small star where grandma lives, another where you live. Two stars make the map personal — and then it gets looked at every day.

      Quick parent note

      Maps answer "where?" long before children can read them properly. A star on a map is a child’s first geography: places are real, they have names, and some of them hold people we love.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Clock Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Classroom object

      The round clock with its two hands — the clock is the day drawn in a circle, and even before reading it, children can learn what its hands mean for them.

      Say it together

      “Clock! Round and round. The long hand runs fast, the short hand walks slow. When the hands say twelve, we eat lunch! When they say three, we tidy up!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Tie the clock to one real moment a day — "when the big hand is up top, snack time!" Say it, wait for it, celebrate when it arrives. One learned moment turns the clock from wall decoration into a promise.

      Quick parent note

      Clock sense grows from routine, not numerals: snack-o’clock comes first, half-past much later. A clock that is talked about is a clock a child will eventually want to read.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Computer Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Classroom object

      The screen on its stand — the computer is the machine that shows letters to trace, songs to sing and stories to hear, and in class it is a tool with a turn.

      Say it together

      “Computer! The big screen. We sit down, we take turns, we use it for a little while. Type a letter… hear the sound… watch the story. All done — screen closes, off we play!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Decide the rule before the screen turns on: what we will do, for how long, and who gets the first turn. A timer makes the ending easy — the timer finishes the turn, not the grown-up saying stop.

      Quick parent note

      A classroom computer is turn-taking practice as much as tech: one seat, one timer, everyone gets a go. The habit of "a little while, then off" is the skill that lasts.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Wastebasket Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 2+Classroom object

      The gray bin in the corner — the wastebasket is where scraps, snips and used-up stickers go, and using it is the easiest real job in the room.

      Say it together

      “Wastebasket! The scrap bin. Paper bit… in it goes! Snip, snip, done? Walk it over… drop… in! The wastebasket says thank you. The room stays lovely.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make clean-up the finishing move of every craft: one basket, one walk, one drop, a small cheer. Who can land the scrap in from one step back? A shot that scores makes tidying the best part of the project.

      Quick parent note

      Own-your-own-mess is a classroom habit that starts with one bin and one proud drop. It also gives every project a real ending, which children like more than adults expect.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Listen Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A boy with his hand to his ear — listening is the first classroom habit, and it looks like still hands, quiet mouth and ears doing the work.

      Say it together

      “Listen! Hand to your ear. What do you hear? The story… the birds… a quiet room. Ears open, mouth quiet, eyes on the book. Now I know you are listening!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the listening game: whisper an instruction across the room — "touch your nose… hop twice… bring the red block." Whispering makes ears work. Then swap: your child whispers, you do the silly move.

      Quick parent note

      Real listening practice is short and fun, not a long lecture about listening. A child who has played at listening knows exactly what the word means when it matters.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Raise Your Hand Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A boy with his arm stretched high — raising a hand is how a big idea gets a turn without talking over friends.

      Say it together

      “Raise your hand! Arm up high — like this! When your hand is up, the teacher sees: "this friend has something to say!" Wait for the nod… and now it is your turn to talk.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Practise at home at story time: anyone with a thought raises a hand and waits to be picked. Make the waiting short and the picking generous — "yes, you wanted to say something!" The habit sticks when turns come round honestly.

      Quick parent note

      Hand-raising is waiting made visible — and waiting is one of the hardest, most valuable skills of the whole early years. Every fair turn a child gets makes the next wait easier.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Follow Directions Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A teacher pointing the way — following directions means hearing the whole instruction and doing it in order: first this, then that, finished means finished.

      Say it together

      “Follow directions! Ears ready? "First hang your coat, THEN come to the rug." Coat… rug… all done! Two steps, both done — that is following directions!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Give two-step missions at home: "put the cup on the table, then sit down." Count the steps on fingers before starting. Two steps done in order earns a high five — then tomorrow, sneak in a third.

      Quick parent note

      Little brains hold one instruction first, two soon after. Asking your child to repeat the steps back — "what comes first?" — turns listening into a plan, which is the whole trick.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Be Kind Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A boy helping a friend up from the floor — being kind is the classroom rule behind every other one, and it is mostly small moves: a hand, a seat, a gentle word.

      Say it together

      “Be kind! A helping hand, a friendly word, a gentle touch. Someone fell? Help them up. Someone is sad? Sit close. Kind hands, kind words — that is how friends are made.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Catch kindness in the act: whenever your child helps, shares or comforts, name it out loud — "that was kind!" Kindness that gets noticed gets repeated. One caught moment a day is plenty.

      Quick parent note

      Children learn kindness by watching it done to them, so the grown-up’s kind voice is the real lesson. Naming kind acts tells a child exactly which of their moves earned the smile.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Share Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      Two children reading one book together — sharing is turning "mine" into "ours," and it is much easier to learn with a timer and a fair plan than with a lecture.

      Say it together

      “Share! One book, two friends. You hold it first… my turn to turn the page… now your turn! Taking turns IS sharing. Look how far one book goes.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Share something real: one colouring page with two crayons, one puzzle, one book with two laps. Say the turn out loud — "your page, my page" — and swap on a count of ten. Fair, short, repeat.

      Quick parent note

      Turn-taking is sharing with visible fairness, and young children need the turns to actually come. Playing together on purpose — one toy, both children — builds the habit better than any reminder.

      From the My Classroom room — with every lesson one tap away.

      FLASHCARD · CLASSROOM · AGES 2–6 YEARS

      Help Others Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      Two children working at one desk — helping others is noticing a friend who is stuck and offering hands before being asked.

      Say it together

      “Help others! See a friend stuck? "I can help!" Two crayons fall — pick one up, hand one back. Helping makes the job small and the friend happy. High five, helpers!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make your child the household helper once a day: carrying the spoons to the table, passing the pegs while you hang washing, holding the door. Real helping — the kind that actually helps — is what builds the identity of "I am a helper."

      Quick parent note

      A child who has been a helper rushes to help others — the label does the work. Give real jobs, not toy ones, and thank the effort louder than the result.

      FLASHCARD · CLASSROOM · AGES 2–6 YEARS

      Say Please Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A boy making a polite request — "please" is the small word at the start of every friendly ask, and it works its magic everywhere from snack time to story time.

      Say it together

      “Say please! "Can I have a snack… PLEASE?" There is the magic word! When you say please, asking sounds kind — and kind asks are the ones that get a yes.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the polite-request game at pretend shops and tea parties, where every order needs a please to be served. Then catch it for real: a genuine "please" at the table gets warm praise and, nearly always, the snack.

      Quick parent note

      Please is easiest to teach at snack time and hardest to remember when a child is desperate — which is exactly when to stay calm and model it. The word sticks with practice, not pressure.

      FLASHCARD · CLASSROOM · AGES 2–6 YEARS

      Say Thank You Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A boy with his hand on his heart, smiling — "thank you" is the word that tells a giver their gift landed, and children love how good it feels to say.

      Say it together

      “Say thank you! Someone gave you a crayon? "Thank you!" Grandma brought a story? "Thank you!" Hand on your heart, big smile — thank you makes the giver happy too.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make thank-you the end of every exchange for one day: snack, help, a passed ball — each one gets its thank you. Then at bedtime, remember together: who did we thank today? Two remembered thank-yous is a lovely day.

      Quick parent note

      Gratitude grows from noticing, and noticing is a habit you can practise out loud. A child who says thank you daily is learning to see the effort of other people — quietly, one snack at a time.

      FLASHCARD · CLASSROOM · AGES 2–6 YEARS

      Use a Quiet Voice Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A boy with a finger to his lips — a quiet voice is the voice classrooms run on, and knowing when it is loud-time and when it is hush-time is a real skill.

      Say it together

      “Use a quiet voice! Finger on lips… shhh. Inside, we use our inside voice — soft and low. Outside? Loud voices, go! But right now we are inside… shhh… can you hear the quiet?”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the voice dial: outside voice on the balcony or in the yard, middle voice in the hall, whisper voice in the car. Name the voice before entering each place — "library voices now!" — and let your child show you the difference.

      Quick parent note

      Volume control is a real skill with a real dial, not a character trait. Giving each place its own voice name turns "be quiet" into a game the child can win.

      FLASHCARD · CLASSROOM · AGES 2–6 YEARS

      Walk Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A boy walking with steady steps — walking feet are for inside, where floors are hard, corners are sharp and running belongs outside.

      Say it together

      “Walk! Inside we walk — one foot, other foot, steady like this. Running feet? Those are for the garden and the park! Inside… walk, walk, walk. Safe and proud.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Practise the switch: at the door, "running feet ready… walking feet ON!" Then walk a straight line together, heel to toe, like tightrope explorers. Make the walking itself the fun part and the rule takes care of itself.

      Quick parent note

      Walking inside is not about slowing down fun — it is about the right place for it. Children who know exactly where running is allowed are far quicker to walk where it is not.

      FLASHCARD · CLASSROOM · AGES 2–6 YEARS

      Clean Up Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Good habit

      A boy returning books to the shelf — clean-up is how play ends well: every block, book and crayon goes home before the next game begins.

      Say it together

      “Clean up! The game is done — now the blocks go home. Block in the box… book on the shelf… crayons in the cup. Sing the clean-up song… look! The room is ready for tomorrow.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Clean up together the first hundred times — never alone. Make it a race against a song, sort by color as you go, and finish with a look-around: "who made this room lovely? YOU did." One basket per toy type makes the whole thing possible.

      Quick parent note

      Clean-up is sorting, matching and finishing, all in one — real maths wearing a chore’s clothes. Children who always clean up with a grown-up learn the routine without learning the dread.

      FLASHCARD · CLASSROOM · AGES 2–6 YEARS

      Keep It Tidy Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4+Good habit

      A tidy desk with everything in its place — keeping it tidy means putting things back as you go, so the next thing always starts easy.

      Say it together

      “Keep it tidy! One paper out, one paper done, one paper away. The pencils sleep in the cup, the books stand on the shelf. A tidy desk says: ready for tomorrow!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      End each work session with the tidy look: crayons cupped, paper stacked, chair pushed in. Snap a photo of the tidy desk once a week — a tidy-spot gallery your child will be proud to grow.

      Quick parent note

      Tidy-as-you-go is a step up from big clean-ups: small resets, often. Children who keep a tidy spot feel ownership of their work — and finding yesterday’s page without a hunt is its own reward.
